title: Azusa Street (1906)
hookLine: a Black preacher, William Seymour, leads a revival in a plain Los Angeles mission building where races worship together

lines: A PREACHER WITH HIS HEAD IN A CRATE.
cards: Sawdust on the floor. Planks laid across boxes for benches. A shabby building on a side street in Los Angeles, once used for storage and, by some accounts, as a stable.
The preacher at the front is a Black man named William Seymour, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye. Sometimes he prays with his head inside an empty wooden crate.

And the room is packed: Black washerwomen, white laborers, Mexican families, newcomers from all over, kneeling side by side, in a country where race usually kept people apart. Newspapers mocked it. People kept coming.

teach.b: The people at Azusa Street said they were living through the Book of Acts again.

On the day of Pentecost, Acts says, the first followers of Jesus were gathered in one place, and in the King James Bible: "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."
At Azusa Street people prayed aloud in tongues, sang without hymnbooks, wept, shouted, fell quiet, and prayed for the sick, day after day.
Pentecostal churches tell it as one of their beginnings, and so do some charismatic Christians in other churches.
Here Christians differ, so plainly: Pentecostals hold that the gifts in Acts, tongues and healing among them, are for today.
Some other Christians believe those gifts belonged mainly to the apostles' time, and worship in quieter ways. Both read the same Bible. Now the line.
A white participant, Frank Bartleman, wrote afterward that at Azusa Street the color line was washed away in the blood, meaning the blood of Christ.
Where race divided churches and much else, a Black preacher led, and people of every color prayed for each other.
Paul had written it long before: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."
The unity didn't last everywhere. In the years after, some churches that grew out of the revival split along the same color line again. That's part of the story.
So is the room where, for a while, it was washed away.

how: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often worship with spontaneous singing, raised hands, prayer for healing and prayer in tongues, and some churches remember Azusa Street as one of their beginnings.

games.q: you're a white laborer in Los Angeles. you walk into the mission and the preacher at the front is a Black man. what do you do?
o: leave. this isn't the kind of church you go to.
stand at the back and watch.
kneel and pray alongside everyone else.
games.why: accounts describe people of every color kneeling and praying together, and Frank Bartleman wrote that the color line was washed away.

practice: Recall the last place you prayed, sang or sat in silence with others, and see who was in the room: who looked like you, and who didn't. Don't judge it; just see it.
Then think of one place nearby where people unlike you gather, and if you pray, pray for that room, or simply hold it in mind.
